svg.aria-label: Diagram: what the two Google Cloud VPC subnet creation modes do at creation time, why every auto mode network sharing one predefined set of IPv4 ranges inside 10.128.0.0/9 makes peering two of them impossible and on-premises overlap likely, why the conversion to custom mode is one-way and still leaves the auto mode expansion ceiling in place, and why converting changes every command that referenced the network implicitly
svg.title: Auto mode versus custom mode: a shared address plan you opt into, and cannot fully leave
svg.text: Auto mode is not a smaller custom mode. It is a shared address plan you opt into.
Every auto mode network everywhere uses the same ranges, which is why two of them can never be joined.
Two creation modes, and what each one does at creation time
AUTO: one subnet from each region is automatically created within it, from predefined IPv4
ranges that fit within the 10.128.0.0/9 CIDR block. New regions arrive as new subnets.
CUSTOM: complete control over its subnets and IP ranges. You decide which subnets to
create in regions that you choose, by using IP ranges that you specify.
The shared block, which is the whole decision
ALL auto mode VPC networks use the same set of IPv4 ranges. Not similar ranges. The same ones.
us-central1 is always 10.128.0.0/20 and us-west1 is always 10.138.0.0/20, in every such network.
So you cannot peer or VPN two auto mode networks together — identical ranges on both sides.
And 10.128.0.0/9 is commonly used RFC 1918 space, so on-premises may already overlap it.
No IPv6 either: IPv6 subnet ranges are not supported on auto mode VPC networks.
The exit is one-way, and it does not undo the geometry
You can convert auto to custom. Conversion from auto to custom mode is a one-way process.
It preserves all of its automatically created subnets, and names and IP ranges are not changed.
Which is the catch: an ex-auto subnet still expands no broader than /16, because anything
broader would conflict with the primary IPv4 ranges of the other automatically created subnets.
Converting relabels the network. It does not give back the address space the mode spent.
And the convenience was in your tooling, not only in the network
Auto mode lets a command omit the subnet, because there is exactly one per region.
After converting, you must review all API calls and gcloud CLI commands that implicitly
reference any subnet that was automatically created while the network was in auto mode.
The --subnet flag is required to reference subnets in a custom mode VPC network.
So the migration is not a network change. It changes everything that calls the network.
Each new project starts with a default network, and that default network is an auto mode network.
So the mode decision is made for you, by default, in every project nobody configured.
The 10.128.0.0/9 block holds 2,048 subnets of /20, so auto mode was never going to run out of
room. It was going to collide — and only with the networks you later wanted to reach.
